title: Start with the shoes
hookLine: in many gurdwaras one honored seva is minding people's shoes
last: NISHKAM SEVA — NO ONE NEEDS TO KNOW.

cards: Muddy sneakers by your own front door. A boot on its side. Somebody's flip-flop under the mat.
Shoes are ordinary, and a little gross. They carry the street into the house. Now go to the entrance of a big gurdwara on a Sunday.
Before anyone goes in, they take off their shoes. Pair after pair after pair. Behind a counter by the door, a line of volunteers takes every pair, hands back a token, and stacks them on shelves.
Some are wiping the shoes clean. And some of those volunteers are people you'd never expect to see there.

teach.h: THE JODA GHAR, THE SHOE HOUSE.
teach.b: The shoe room at a gurdwara has a name: the joda ghar, the shoe house. Sikhs count minding it as an honored seva. That can surprise a visitor.
Why would the dirtiest job be the honored one? Because of what shoes mean.
In the Punjab the Gurus knew, as in many places, feet and shoes were counted the lowest things, where caste and pride said you must never put your hands. The Guru Granth Sahib turns that upside down.

teach.h: THE DUST OF THE FEET OF THE HOLY.
teach.b: Again and again the Gurus ask for the dust of the feet of the holy, the humblest place there is. So whoever takes your shoes and cleans them is taking the lowest place on purpose.
It's nishkam seva, yesterday's word, in its plainest form. Nobody remembers who held their shoes.
And when the Akal Takht, the Sikh community's central authority, asks someone to make amends for a wrong, the penance can include cleaning shoes and washing dishes at the gurdwara.
It has been asked even of powerful politicians.
The shoes are a great leveler. You can't do this seva and stay proud for long. Try handing a stranger their muddy boots with a smile.

This week ran from a letter to an emperor, through a book made Guru, water for the enemy, a needle and one light, to a rack of shoes by the door. Camp three starts there: at the door, on the floor, at the bottom.

how: Visitors take off their shoes before entering a gurdwara, and volunteers in the joda ghar, the shoe room, look after them, often cleaning them, as a humble and honored seva.

games.q: you've come to a gurdwara to help, and there are two jobs left: reading notices from the stage, or taking people's shoes at the door. which do Sikhs count as an honored seva?
o: the stage, where everyone can see you.
games.why: Sikhs count minding shoes in the joda ghar an honored seva, precisely because it's the lowest place.

practice: If you can, kneel by the shoes at your door and pair them up, yours first and then someone else's, wiping off a little mud if you like. Go slowly, and if a small feeling says this is beneath you, let it be there.
If you can't get up right now, picture your hands tidying them, one pair at a time.

wordCard.voice: Joda ghar. The shoe house at a gurdwara, where minding strangers' shoes is an honored seva. Your week: the Zafarnama, the Granth as Guru, water for the enemy, the needle, jot, nishkam seva, and the shoes.
